sections.heading: Spanish is spelled the way it sounds
sections.body:
Good news: Spanish spelling is very regular. Once you know how each letter sounds, you can read almost any word aloud correctly, even one you have never seen.

The five vowels are always short and clear, and they never change: *a* as in "father", *e* as in "bet", *i* as in "machine", *o* as in "more" (but shorter), *u* as in "rule". Say *casa*, *mesa*, *sí*, *no*, *uno* and listen to how pure each vowel is.

sections.heading: The alphabet
sections.body: The Spanish alphabet has 27 letters: the 26 you know plus *ñ*. Letter names are useful for spelling your name or an email address. In much of Latin America you'll also hear *be larga* or *be grande* for B, *ve corta* or *ve chica* for V, and *doble ve* for W; the RAE-recommended names in the table are understood everywhere. *Ye* used to be called *i griega*, and many people still say that.

sections.heading: Consonants that differ from English
sections.body:
- *h* is always silent: *hola* sounds like "ola".
- *j* is a breathy sound from the throat, like a strong English h: *jugo*, *José*.
- *g* before *e* or *i* sounds like *j* (*gente*); before *a*, *o*, *u* it is hard like in "go" (*gato*).
- *c* before *e* or *i* sounds like s in Latin America (*cena*); otherwise it is k (*casa*). *z* also sounds like s (*zapato*).
- *ll* and *y* sound like the y in "yes" in most of Latin America: *llamo*, *yo*.
- *ñ* is like the ny in "canyon": *niño*, *mañana*.
- *r* is a quick single tap, like the tt in American "butter": *pero*. *rr*, and *r* at the start of a word, is rolled: *perro*, *rojo*.
- *qu* sounds like k (the u is silent): *queso*, *que*.
- *b* and *v* sound the same: *vaca* and *baca* are pronounced identically.
- *d* between vowels is soft, like the th in "this": *nada*.

sections.heading: Stress and written accents
sections.body:
Every Spanish word has one stressed syllable, and the rules tell you where it is:

- Words ending in a vowel, *n* or *s* stress the second-to-last syllable: *casa* (CA-sa), *hablan*.
- Words ending in any other consonant stress the last syllable: *hablar* (ha-BLAR), *papel*.
- A written accent (´) breaks the rule and marks the stressed syllable: *café*, *música*, *lápiz*.

Some short words use an accent only to tell two meanings apart: *sí* (yes) and *si* (if), *tú* (you) and *tu* (your). Questions and exclamations open with upside-down marks: *¿…?* and *¡…!*

sections.heading: Spelling out loud
sections.body: To spell a word, say the letter names: *hola* is *hache, o, ele, a*. To ask how something is spelled, say *¿Cómo se escribe?* (How is it written?).
